slides.0.title: Deep Dive into Tokaj
slides.0.subtitle: The Birth of the World's Greatest Sweet Wine: The Aszú System and the Dry Revolution
slides.1.title: Tokaj Wine Region: Full Geographic Overview
slides.1.componentProps.description: The Tokaj UNESCO World Heritage wine region spans 27 villages. The autumn morning fog that settles in the Bodrog and Tisza river valleys is the natural incubator for noble rot.
slides.2.title: The Miracle of Noble Rot: The Magic of Botrytis Cinerea
slides.2.highlights.0.title: What is Noble Rot?
slides.2.highlights.0.content: The Botrytis Cinerea fungus penetrates the grape skin, causing moisture to evaporate and sugars to concentrate. Under the right conditions this is "Noble Rot" — a winemaker's most precious ally
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Tokaj's Perfect Conditions
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Autumn morning fog from the Bodrog and Tisza valleys provides moisture for fungal growth; warm, dry afternoons evaporate that moisture, preventing grey rot
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Chemical Transformation
slides.2.highlights.2.content: After moisture evaporation, sugar concentration can reach 450–800 g/L (normal grapes contain just 200–250 g/L); glycerol, acidity and aromatic compounds concentrate simultaneously
slides.2.highlights.3.title: Hand-Picking Aszú Berries
slides.2.highlights.3.content: Only fully botrytis-infected berries (Aszú Berries) can be harvested — individually by hand — an enormously labour-intensive and costly process
slides.2.content:
The "miracle of botrytis" that takes place in Tokaj each autumn is the result of a precise interplay of geography, climate and timing — one of the wine world's most remarkable natural phenomena.

🦠 The Four-Step Botrytis Process

Step 1
Morning fog (Aug–Oct): Fog from the Bodrog and Tisza valleys settles on the grapes; fungal hyphae penetrate the thin Furmint skin.
Step 2
Warm, dry afternoon: Sunlight evaporates the moisture; grapes begin to shrivel; sugar, acid and glycerol concentrate enormously.
Step 3
Aszú berry forms: Fully infected berries turn dark brown and raisin-like — the Aszú berry is born.
Step 4
Multiple hand-picking passes: Workers enter the vineyard 3–7 times, selecting only the ripest Aszú berries each time.

📊 Normal Grape vs Aszú Berry

Normal GrapeAszú Berry
Sugar200–250 g/L450–800 g/L
JuicePlentifulBarely any
ColourClear goldDark brown / wrinkled
slides.3.title: The Aszú Classification System: The Puttonyos Scale
slides.3.highlights.0.title: What is a Puttonyos?
slides.3.highlights.0.content: "Puttonyos" is the traditional wooden backpack tub used to carry harvested Aszú berries — each tub holds approximately 20 kg
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Sweetness Grades
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Traditionally 3–6 Puttonyos (indicating how many tubs of Aszú paste were added per 136 litres of base wine); the higher the number, the sweeter the wine
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Modern Reform (2013)
slides.3.highlights.2.content: From 2013 regulations were simplified: only a residual sugar of ≥120 g/L is required; the specific Puttonyos number is no longer mandated
slides.3.highlights.3.title: Eszencia: The Legendary Essence
slides.3.highlights.3.content: The tiny amount of juice pressed by the sheer weight of Aszú berries alone; sugar levels reach 450–800 g/L; produced only in the finest years
slides.3.content:
The Puttonyos system is Tokaj's historic measure of sweetness — one of the wine world's most evocative grading traditions.

📊 The Four Sweetness Levels

3 Puttonyos
Residual sugar: 60–90 g/L
Entry sweetness — noticeable but not heavy
4 Puttonyos
Residual sugar: 90–120 g/L
Medium sweetness — growing complexity
5 Puttonyos
Residual sugar: 120–150 g/L
Rich and sweet — honey and apricot dominant
6 Puttonyos
Residual sugar: 150+ g/L
Highest grade — candied orange peel, coffee, beeswax

💎 Eszencia — The World's Rarest Wine

  • Pure Aszú berry juice pressed by gravity alone — no mechanical pressure
  • Sugar: 450–800 g/L (thicker than honey)
  • Alcohol: usually only 2–5% (extreme sugar limits fermentation)
  • Requires 3–5+ years in barrel before bottling
  • Legend holds that Habsburg emperors were revived from their deathbed by Eszencia
slides.4.title: Dry Furmint: Tokaj's New Identity in the 21st Century
slides.4.highlights.0.title: From Sweet to Dry
slides.4.highlights.0.content: After the 1990s, a group of winemakers began exploring Furmint's potential for dry wines, challenging the stereotype that "Tokaj means sweet wine only"
slides.4.highlights.1.title: International Recognition
slides.4.highlights.1.content: Top dry Furmints now score 90+ points in Wine Spectator and Decanter; exceptional vintages can exceed 95 points
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Compared to White Burgundy
slides.4.highlights.2.content: Many describe top dry Furmint as similar to great white Burgundy: high acidity, minerality, creamy texture and exceptional ageing potential
slides.4.highlights.3.title: Leading Export Ambassador
slides.4.highlights.3.content: Dry Furmint is growing rapidly in the UK, German and US markets, becoming Hungary's most important wine export ambassador
slides.4.content:
Dry Furmint is perhaps Hungary's most exciting contemporary wine story — a grape once exclusively associated with sweet wine revealing an entirely new dimension.

🍾 Three Stages of Dry Furmint Evolution

Young (1–3 years)
  • Lime, green apple, white peach
  • Pronounced mineral / flint notes
  • High acid, vibrant freshness
  • Ideal with fish and seafood
Mature (5–10 years)
  • Honey, beeswax, ripe apricot
  • Toasted hazelnut, cream, smoke
  • More complex minerality
  • Comparable to top white Burgundy
Old Vine (15+ years)
  • Brown spices, gingerbread, orange peel
  • Extraordinarily complex mineral-oxidative notes
  • Remarkable ageing performance
  • Top vintages can last 30+ years

🏅 Top Dry Furmint Producers

Patricius Winery · Tokaj Nobilis · Holdvölgy Estate · Oremus (Vega Sicilia) · Sauska · Áts Károly
slides.5.title: 1737: A Classification System 118 Years Before Bordeaux
slides.5.highlights.0.title: The World's First Official Classification
slides.5.highlights.0.content: In 1737, Habsburg Emperor Charles VI decreed that Tokaj's vineyards be formally divided into three quality tiers (First Class, Second Class, Third Class)
slides.5.highlights.1.title: 118 Years Before Bordeaux
slides.5.highlights.1.content: Bordeaux's famous 1855 Médoc Classification was established in 1855 — 118 years after Tokaj's pioneering system
slides.5.highlights.2.title: Simultaneous Trade Protection (1737)
slides.5.highlights.2.content: The same decree prohibited outside wines from being sold within the Tokaj region — effectively creating the world's earliest AOC-style system
slides.5.highlights.3.title: Royal Patronage
slides.5.highlights.3.content: The Habsburgs, the Russian Tsars and the French court were all devoted fans; Louis XIV called it "the Wine of Kings, King of Wines"
slides.5.content:
Tokaj's classification story is a remarkable testament to how a single wine region can shape the entire history of wine regulation.

📜 Tokaj Historical Timeline

1630s
Máté Szepsy Laczkó produces the first documented botrytis Aszú wine
1703
The Rákóczi family sends Tokaji Aszú to the French court; Louis XIV declares it "Wine of Kings, King of Wines"
1737
Emperor Charles VI's decree establishes the world's first official vineyard classification
1855
Bordeaux's Médoc classification is established — 118 years after Tokaj
1989
Hungary opens its market; foreign capital enters (AXA, Vega Sicilia)
2002
Tokaj Wine Region Historic Cultural Landscape inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site
slides.6.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
What roles do Tokaj's autumn morning fog and warm dry afternoons each play in botrytis development?
A. Both fog and afternoon warmth promote fungal growth simultaneously
B. The fog provides moisture so hyphae can penetrate the grape skin; the warm afternoon evaporates water, concentrating sugars and preventing grey rot
C. The fog prevents the grapes from over-ripening; afternoon warmth stops fungal growth
D. Morning fog lowers temperatures; afternoon warmth is irrelevant

Tokaj's microclimate works in two complementary phases: morning fog from the river valleys raises humidity, allowing Botrytis Cinerea hyphae to penetrate the thin Furmint skins; then warm, dry afternoons evaporate the moisture, concentrating the sugars and flavours and preventing the rot from turning grey (destructive). This alternation is the essential engine of Aszú production.
What does "6 Puttonyos" Tokaji Aszú signify?
A. The wine was aged in 6 different types of barrel
B. The wine was harvested over 6 separate picking passes
C. Traditionally, 6 tubs (puttonyos) of Aszú paste were added per 136 litres of base wine — the highest sweetness level
D. The wine has 6% residual sugar

In the traditional Puttonyos system, each tub (puttonyos) of Aszú paste added per 136-litre barrel of base wine increased the sweetness level. Six Puttonyos represented the maximum — an intensely sweet, concentrated wine with residual sugar exceeding 150 g/L. Since the 2013 reform, the specific Puttonyos number is no longer required; instead, a minimum residual sugar of 120 g/L qualifies a wine as Tokaji Aszú.
What is the key difference between dry Furmint and Tokaji Aszú?
A. Dry Furmint uses Hárslevelű; Aszú uses Furmint
B. Dry Furmint is fully fermented with residual sugar below 4 g/L; Aszú uses botrytis-concentrated berries with residual sugar of 120–800 g/L
C. Aszú and dry Furmint are made from the same juice — only the ageing method differs
D. Dry Furmint comes only from Somló; Aszú comes only from Tokaj

The fundamental distinction is the winemaking process and resulting sugar level. Dry Furmint is fermented to dryness (below 4 g/L residual sugar), expressing the grape's naturally high acidity and volcanic mineral character. Tokaji Aszú is made from botrytis-shrivelled berries whose sugars are so concentrated (450–800 g/L) that fermentation cannot consume them all, resulting in residual sugar of at least 120 g/L.
In which year did Tokaj establish its vineyard classification, making it 118 years before Bordeaux?

In 1737, Habsburg Emperor Charles VI issued a decree formally classifying Tokaj's vineyards into three quality tiers — First Class, Second Class and Third Class. This was the world's first official vineyard classification system. Bordeaux's celebrated 1855 Médoc classification came 118 years later (1855 − 1737 = 118). The same 1737 decree also prohibited non-Tokaj wines from being sold within the region, making it arguably the world's earliest AOC-equivalent system.
